Neonates of the Yellow-bellied mud turtle emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a carapace length at birth measuring just 3 centimeters [Lb = 3 centimeters], a diminutive size that underscores the vulnerability of the hatchling stage in this species. Field surveys conducted in the coastal wetlands of southeastern Africa indicate that yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous reserves during the first weeks of life, a period defined by progressive yolk utilization and shell pipping. The onset of exogenous feeding, marked by the first successful prey capture, typically occurs several days after complete yolk-sac resorption, at which point the young juvenile must actively forage for aquatic invertebrates and small fish. This early life history phase is characterized by rapid somatic growth, with individuals doubling their linear dimensions within the first few months under favorable conditions, although mortality remains substantial due to predation by piscivorous birds and large amphibians. The transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an actively feeding juvenile represents a critical developmental bottleneck, and the modest hatchling size likely constrains the range of available prey items until the carapace hardens sufficiently to offer structural defense.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been recorded at approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days], a protracted maturation period consistent with the slow life-history pace observed among pelomedusid turtles. This developmental delay reflects the substantial energetic investment required to attain the body size necessary for successful reproduction, with juveniles gradually transitioning through a prolonged sub-adult phase characterized by continued carapace growth and the acquisition of adult coloration. During this interval, immature individuals exhibit a mixed feeding strategy that shifts progressively from omnivory toward a more carnivorous diet as they grow, likely driven by the changing profitability of different prey types. The attainment of sexual maturation is marked by gonadal activation and the onset of gametogenesis, events that in wild populations appear to coincide with the onset of the wet season, suggesting that environmental cues—particularly thermal and hydrological regimes—modulate the timing of reproductive development.

Fully grown adults of Pelusios castanoides achieve an ultimate carapace length of approximately 17 centimeters [Li = approximately 17 centimeters], a moderate body size that situates this species within the mid-range of the genus. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a reproductively active adult reaches about 1795 grams [Wwi = about 1795 grams], a mass that reflects the robust, high-domed shell and substantial soft-tissue investment characteristic of this predominantly aquatic chelonian. This adult body mass is notably greater than that recorded for several congeneric species occupying similar habitats, suggesting that Pelusios castanoides may exploit a relatively productive trophic niche that permits sustained energy accumulation. Gravid females, in particular, undergo considerable mass gain during the pre-oviposition period as they develop a clutch of large, yolk-laden eggs, with individual body weight fluctuating markedly across the reproductive cycle. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in overall size, with females typically attaining larger ultimate dimensions than males, a pattern attributed to the selective pressures imposed by fecundity and the physical demands of egg carriage and nesting.

The lifespan of the Yellow-bellied mud turtle has been estimated at 40 years [am = 40 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] in captivity, a longevity that aligns with the general pattern of extended life spans observed in slow-maturing freshwater turtles with low adult mortality rates. This substantial maximum longevity allows individuals to accumulate multiple reproductive opportunities over a long adult phase, offsetting the high mortality experienced during the early life stages. Reproductive senescence, characterized by a gradual decline in clutch size and hatching success, has been documented in older females, though the age at which such declines become detectable varies considerably among captive individuals. Physiological death typically occurs following a period of progressive deterioration in organ function, often associated with the accumulation of age-related pathologies affecting the kidneys and cardiovascular system. The species' capacity for extended survival under controlled conditions underscores the importance of thermal environment in modulating aging rates, with cooler temperatures generally correlating with slower metabolic decline and potentially even greater longevity.

In terms of annual reproductive output, females studied under captive conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], each clutch containing approximately 6 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 6 eggs]. This modest reproductive rate, equivalent to roughly 6 eggs per year when considering the annual frequency, is characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy typical of many long-lived freshwater turtles. The nesting season in southeastern African populations coincides with the early rainy season, when soil moisture facilitates excavation of the nest cavity and subsequent incubation of the leathery-shelled eggs over a period of 60 to 90 days. Hatching success in natural nests is highly variable, influenced by predation from monitor lizards and mammals, as well as by fluctuations in temperature and humidity that can disrupt embryonic development. Despite the low annual fecundity relative to many other reptiles, the species' high adult survival and prolonged reproductive lifespan ensure that lifetime reproductive output remains substantial, contributing to the demographic stability of local populations.
